prime.problem: BLEU was the standard way to score generated text against a reference. For code it can reward a program that's wrong by one character and punish a correct program written differently.
prime.fits: The foil for the whole paper. Functional correctness and pass@k exist because this metric fails; this card shows exactly how, with the same has_dup samples.
prime.goal: Compute BLEU from n-gram counts, explain why it ranks a wrong sample above a correct one, and say where BLEU is still the right tool.

attend: What does each p_n count, and why does one flipped operator cost so little of it?
Why does the correct alternative algorithm B score 0 rather than something low but positive?
What exactly does Figure 8 show, and what does the paper not claim from it?
In which settings does BLEU still make sense even for code?

must: BLEU = brevity penalty × geometric mean of 1- to 4-gram precisions → it counts shared token runs with a reference → a one-token change breaks only the few n-grams that include it → sample C keeps 78.3
Geometric mean with no smoothing → any p_n = 0 makes BLEU 0 → a correct program with a different algorithm and no shared 4-grams scores 0
Correct and wrong Codex samples overlap in BLEU (Figure 8) → BLEU gains may not mean correctness gains → the paper grades by tests instead
BLEU needs only references, no execution → cheap, no sandbox → still useful for docstrings, translation, or code you can't safely run
elevated: CodeBLEU adds keyword, AST and data-flow matching → closer to structure but still not behaviour → it would still miss a flipped == that keeps the AST shape
reference: the exact tokenisation used in the example

compress.prompt: From memory, write the BLEU formula in words, then explain in 2–3 sentences why it ranks the has_dup samples A > C > B while tests rank A = B > C.
checklist: BLEU = BP × exp(average of log p₁…p₄)
p_n = clipped matching n-grams / n-grams in the sample
C shares almost every n-gram with the reference, so scores high
B shares no 4-gram, so the unsmoothed score is 0
tests judge behaviour: A and B pass, C fails

retrieve.q: Explain what BLEU was designed to measure, and why that design fits translation better than code.
answer: overlap of word runs with a reference translation
in translation, near-equivalent phrasings share many n-grams
in code, tiny edits flip behaviour and correct rewrites share few n-grams

retrieve.q: Walk through computing BLEU for sample C from its counts 13/14, 11/13, 9/12, 7/11 with BP = 1.
answer: exp of the average ≈ 0.783, so BLEU ≈ 78.3

retrieve.q: You're evaluating a docstring-generation model with no way to run the described code. Would you use BLEU? What would you pair it with?
answer: BLEU is reasonable: there's a reference and no tests
pair with human grading on a sample, as the paper did for Codex-D
don't read small BLEU gains as quality gains

compare.q: On the same three samples, BLEU and tests disagree about B and C. Which property of each metric causes each disagreement?
answer: BLEU scores surface overlap; tests score outputs on chosen inputs
B: low overlap, same behaviour, so BLEU punishes it
C: high overlap, opposite behaviour, so BLEU rewards it

compare.q: Codex-D produces English, where BLEU is at home, yet the paper still grades it by hand. Why?
answer: the question is whether the docstring specifies the code uniquely and accurately
a docstring can overlap the reference and still miss a crucial detail
so even for text, overlap isn't the property being tested

predict.q: Apply 'add-one' smoothing to sample B's precisions (so 0/22 becomes 1/23). Would B's BLEU rise above C's 78.3? Commit, then reveal.
predict.answer: No. Smoothing only rescues B from exactly 0; its precisions (5/25, 2/24, 1/23 and a smoothed ~1/23) are all tiny, so its geometric mean stays in the single digits. The ranking C over B is caused by low overlap, not by the zero, so smoothing can't fix what the paper objects to.

apply.task: Break BLEU on your own: write a short reference function, a correct rewrite that uses a different approach, and a wrong version that changes one token. Count their 1-gram and 2-gram matches against the reference, and show the wrong version outscoring the correct one on at least one of those precisions.
apply.done: You have three snippets and a small table of p₁ and p₂ where the one-token-wrong version beats the correct rewrite, plus one test that separates them.
apply.hint: Something like return x > 0 vs return not x <= 0 vs return x < 0 works.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: whether smoothing rescues B?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the geometric mean makes a single zero fatal?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: n-gram overlap → BLEU, or BLEU → (not) correctness?
The paper's evidence is one figure on 4 tasks. How strongly would you phrase its conclusion?
Where would you still reach for BLEU in your own work?
